name: Irisin

lead: Irisin is a protein proposed in 2012 to be released by exercising muscle and to turn white fat toward a brown-fat-like, heat-producing state, burning more calories. Fat-loss readers cite it as a way exercise might make you leaner.

It is cleaved from the membrane protein FNDC5, whose production rises with muscle PGC-1-alpha, and cell and animal studies propose signalling through alpha-V integrin receptors. The browning finding comes from mice; researchers have disputed how reliably irisin can be measured in people, and human studies mainly measure blood levels.

paras: There is no product; people associate irisin with regular exercise as the thing that raises it. Discussion centres on training as the lever.
No approved product exists and no human safety data for administering irisin are described in the sources reviewed.

angle.text: Irisin is a proposed exercise hormone: muscle releases it during training, and in mice it turns white fat brown-like and raises energy expenditure, pointing to a leaner look. Human evidence is limited and disputed.

lead: Irisin is a protein fragment cleaved from FNDC5 (fibronectin type III domain-containing protein 5) and was proposed in 2012 as a hormone released by muscle during exercise. Boström and colleagues reported in Nature that it was PGC-1-alpha-dependent and drove brown-fat-like changes in white fat tissue in mice.[1][2]

The proposal attracted wide attention for possible links to weight loss and diabetes prevention, and it also drew sustained scepticism about whether irisin exists in meaningful circulating amounts in humans and whether commercial assays measure it reliably.[2]
Irisin is an endogenous protein. The sources reviewed describe no approved drug, and human evidence is largely observational measurement of blood levels.

paras: FNDC5 was first found in 2002 through genome searches for fibronectin type III domains. In January 2012 Boström et al. described a cleaved form that they named irisin and linked to exercise, PGC-1-alpha and thermogenic (UCP1-expressing) fat.[1][2]
Related work in the same year described beige adipocytes as a distinct thermogenic fat cell type in mice and humans.[3]

In animal and cell studies, irisin has been reported to promote browning of white fat, including through p38 and ERK signalling.[4] A 2018 study reported that irisin acts on bone and fat through alpha-V integrin receptors.[5] In mice, the exercise-linked PGC-1-alpha/FNDC5 pathway was also reported to raise hippocampal BDNF.[6]
A human study reported that irisin and FGF21 rise in response to cold exposure and are associated with brown-fat function.[7]

Several groups questioned the original findings, including whether commercial antibody assays measure irisin accurately and whether the human FNDC5 start codon permits normal production of the protein. A later mass-spectrometry study reported irisin in human plasma, and a 2024 study reported translation of FNDC5 from an upstream start codon.[2] Researchers have studied the predictors of circulating FNDC5/irisin and its response to weight loss and exercise in humans.[8]

No studies found testing irisin itself as an appearance or fat-loss treatment. Registered human studies are observational or measure irisin as an outcome, such as serum irisin in acne patients taking isotretinoin, and its temporal dynamics during exercise.[9][10]

timeline.event: FNDC5 first identified in genome searches.[2]
Boström et al. propose irisin as an exercise-induced myokine that browns white fat.[1]
Mass spectrometry study reports irisin in human plasma.[2]
Alpha-V integrins reported as irisin receptors in bone and fat.[5]
